theory.heading: Understand workability
theory.body: Workability describes how a material responds to approved shaping, joining and finishing processes. It is not a fixed label that applies equally in every situation. A material may respond differently depending on its properties, condition, the approved tools and the process being used. Workability should be judged from evidence rather than from assumptions such as softwood is always easy to work or dense timber is always difficult. Current school SOPs and teacher directions control all actual workshop activity.

theory.heading: Observe material evidence
theory.body: A useful material description begins with careful observation. Grain describes the direction and pattern of the wood fibres. Knots show where branches grew and may change the nearby grain. Texture describes how the surface looks or feels, such as smooth, coarse or uneven. Density is mass in relation to volume. Students can also record observed behaviour during teacher-approved activities, such as whether the material responded evenly or showed noticeable variation. These observations should describe what happened without claiming more than the evidence supports.

theory.heading: Build a supported description
theory.body: An evidence-based description combines several relevant observations instead of relying on one feature. A student might describe mostly straight grain, one visible knot, a moderately smooth texture and variation near the knot during an approved process. This is more useful than simply calling the material good, bad, strong or easy. The condition of the sample, the approved tool and the process must also be considered because each can affect the result. When evidence is unclear or limited, state the uncertainty and ask rather than inventing an explanation.

questions.question: What does workability describe?
choices: How a material responds to approved shaping, joining and finishing processes
The exact age of the timber
The colour of the finished project
The number of tools in the workshop
questions.correctFeedback: Correct. Workability describes how a material responds during approved processes.
questions.retryFeedback: Review Understand workability and focus on the opening definition.

questions.question: Why is workability not a fixed label?
choices: Every material behaves exactly the same
The response can depend on properties, condition, tools and process
Only timber colour affects it
It can only be judged from the tree species name
questions.correctFeedback: Correct. Several factors can change how a material responds in a particular situation.
questions.retryFeedback: Return to Understand workability and identify the factors that influence material response.

questions.question: Which statement is an unsupported assumption?
choices: The material responded evenly during an approved activity
The sample has visible knots
All softwood is always easy to work
The surface appears uneven
questions.correctFeedback: Correct. A botanical category alone does not prove how workable every sample will be.
questions.retryFeedback: Re-read Understand workability and focus on the examples of assumptions that should be avoided.

questions.question: What does grain describe?
choices: The smoothness of a finish
The mass of a timber sample
The age of a knot
The direction and pattern of wood fibres
questions.correctFeedback: Correct. Grain describes the direction and visible pattern of the fibres.
questions.retryFeedback: Review Observe material evidence and locate the definition of grain.

questions.question: What does texture describe?
choices: The botanical group of the tree
How the surface looks or feels
The volume of the sample
The location of a branch
questions.correctFeedback: Correct. Texture describes surface qualities such as smoothness, coarseness or unevenness.
questions.retryFeedback: Return to Observe material evidence and focus on the surface feature described there.

questions.question: Which observation best describes material behaviour?
choices: The timber is definitely strong
The sample will always be suitable
The material responded evenly during an approved activity
The knot proves poor quality
questions.correctFeedback: Correct. This statement records observed behaviour without adding an unsupported conclusion.
questions.retryFeedback: Re-read Observe material evidence and focus on how observed behaviour should be recorded.

questions.question: Why should students avoid claiming more than the evidence supports?
choices: Density explains every property
All timber samples are identical
Only the teacher may observe texture
Material descriptions should separate observation from assumption
questions.correctFeedback: Correct. Evidence-based descriptions report what can be observed without inventing conclusions.
questions.retryFeedback: Review the final sentence of Observe material evidence and identify the limit placed on conclusions.

questions.question: Which description uses several pieces of evidence?
choices: The sample has mostly straight grain, one knot and a moderately smooth texture
The timber is easy
The material is good
The material must be strong
questions.correctFeedback: Correct. This description combines specific observations instead of using a vague judgement.
questions.retryFeedback: Return to Build a supported description and locate the example combining several material features.

questions.question: Why must the sample condition, approved tool and process be considered?
choices: They remove the need to observe grain
They change softwood into hardwood
Each can affect the observed result
They guarantee the same response every time
questions.correctFeedback: Correct. Material response can vary when the sample condition, tool or process changes.
questions.retryFeedback: Re-read Build a supported description and focus on the factors that can affect the result.

questions.question: What should a student do when material evidence is unclear?
choices: Invent the most likely explanation
Copy another student's description
Describe the material as poor quality
State the uncertainty and ask
questions.correctFeedback: Correct. Recognising uncertainty is more accurate than inventing an unsupported explanation.
questions.retryFeedback: Review the final sentence of Build a supported description and identify the response to limited evidence.

written.prompt: Write an evidence-based description of a timber sample using grain, knots, texture, density information and one observed behaviour from an approved activity.
written.sentenceStarter: The sample has ___ grain, ___ knots and a ___ texture. The density information shows ___. During the approved activity, I observed ___.
written.example: The sample has mostly straight grain, one visible knot and a moderately smooth texture. The available density information suggests it is denser than the comparison sample. During the approved activity, it responded evenly except near the knot.
